Four days on the engineering that turns a model call into a product: architecture,
structure, guardrails, evaluation, and unit economics. The course is built around
one artefact you extend all week — **Murshid (مرشد)**, a bilingual citizen-services
assistant — so by Thursday afternoon the "project" is assembly and one extension,
not a fresh build.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Everything runs offline

No API key, no network, no GPU. The repository ships a course gateway that speaks
both provider dialects and answers from rules, so every lab, test and evaluation
run works on a laptop on a plane — and every drill (the rate-limit storm, the
provider outage) fires on command instead of when a provider happens to have a bad
afternoon.

Pointing a route at a real provider is two environment variables and no code
change. That substitution is not a convenience; it is the argument of Module 1,
and you will perform it rather than be told about it.
:::

## What you leave with

| Discipline | The thing you build | The evidence it works |
|---|---|---|
| **Architecture** | A router-first application with every model call behind one boundary | A provider swap that is a config edit, proven under a fault drill |
| **Structure** | Validated `ServiceTicket` extraction and a bounded tool loop | Schema-pass rate by language; four negative safety tests |
| **Guardrails** | A three-layer input wall and a canary output wall | Block rate **and** false-positive rate, reported together, always |
| **Evaluation** | A 126-case stratified bilingual golden set, a calibrated judge, a CI gate | A seeded prompt regression blocked with slice evidence |
| **Cost** | A meter, prompt-cache discipline, a two-tier cache, routing with a cascade | 4.07 → 0.37 halalas per conversation, green at every step |
| **Comparison** | The same suite against commercial and open-weight backends | A routing recommendation with a break-even, not a leaderboard quote |

## The four days

::: {.grid}

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### Day 1 — From demo to system
Why LLM applications fail differently. Four architecture patterns and when each is
justified. The model boundary. Then two providers behind one interface, streaming
with time-to-first-token measured, and a retry policy that survives a live 429
storm.

[Module 1](modules/m1-architecture.qmd) · [Lab 1](labs/lab1-skeleton.qmd) ·
[Module 2](modules/m2-apis-and-open-weights.qmd) · [Lab 2](labs/lab2-two-providers.qmd)
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### Day 2 — Structure and control
Structured outputs that are validated rather than hoped for, and the
validate → retry → repair loop. Then tools: schemas the model uses correctly, a
bounded execution loop, and an authorisation gate that no sequence of conversation
turns can talk its way past.

[Module 3](modules/m3-structured-outputs-and-tools.qmd) ·
[Lab 3](labs/lab3-tickets-and-tools.qmd) ·
[Module 4](modules/m4-prompts-and-guardrails.qmd)
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### Day 3 — Prove it, then pay less for it
Prompts as versioned artefacts. Injection defence in layers, measured honestly.
Golden sets that earn trust, a judge you qualify before you trust, a gate that
blocks the regression code review cannot see — and only then, optimisation.

[Lab 4](labs/lab4-guarded-pipeline.qmd) · [Module 5](modules/m5-evaluation.qmd) ·
[Lab 5](labs/lab5-evaluation-harness.qmd) ·
[Module 6](modules/m6-cost-latency-caching.qmd) · [Lab 6](labs/lab6-optimise.qmd)
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### Day 4 — Ship the application
Integration, a peer architecture review, the full harness on both backends, a
cost budget you have to meet, a red-team round from the pair next to you, and a
five-minute demo that takes an adversarial question from the floor.

[Capstone](capstone.qmd) · [Assessment](assessment.qmd)
:::

:::

## The one sentence

> Never trade quality you aren't measuring for cost you are.

Everything in Module 6 follows from it, and most of Modules 4 and 5 exist to make
the first half of the sentence possible.

## Start here

```bash
git clone https://github.com/MohammadYusif/llm-application-engineering
cd llm-application-engineering/murshid
docker compose up -d          # gateway + redis + the application
make doctor                   # python, config, Arabic rendering, every route
make chat
```

Full instructions, including the Windows path and what to do when `doctor` prints a
cross, are on the [setup page](setup.qmd).

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Prerequisites
SDA-AIE-111. SDA-FND-102 recommended. You should be comfortable writing Python and
reading someone else's; you do not need to have used an LLM API before.
:::
